snapshots.name: George Washington
snapshots.subtitle: President of the Constitutional Convention
snapshots.body: Named as the president of the 1787 convention that drafted the federal Constitution — Tocqueville notes the assembly that produced America's fundamental law was small in number but contained the country's choicest political talent.

snapshots.name: Thomas Jefferson
snapshots.subtitle: 'The greatest Democrat America has yet produced'
snapshots.body: Cited repeatedly, including his own private letters on the instability of American law, and described elsewhere in the book as the greatest Democrat America has yet produced — an authority Tocqueville treats as unusually candid about democracy's defects as well as its promise.

snapshots.name: Andrew Jackson
snapshots.subtitle: A weak president elected by military glory
snapshots.body: Discussed as the president twice elected by the Americans on the strength of his military reputation alone — for Tocqueville, a case study in how the popular passion for glory can hand power to a man he judges to have shown little talent as chief magistrate.

snapshots.name: Alexander Hamilton
snapshots.subtitle: Federalist voice cited on executive power
snapshots.body: Named as one of the principal founders of the Constitution, quoted from The Federalist on the strengths of a single executive — one of the authorities Tocqueville draws on to diagnose both the powers and the dangers built into the American constitutional design.

snapshots.name: James Madison
snapshots.subtitle: Correspondent on the instability of laws
snapshots.body: Appears as the recipient of Jefferson's letter on the instability of American laws, and elsewhere as one of the framers Tocqueville treats as an authoritative witness to the Constitution's original intentions and internal tensions.

snapshots.name: The Puritans
snapshots.subtitle: Founders of New England
snapshots.body: The English emigrants — Tocqueville notes they called themselves Pilgrims — whose austere religious principles earned them this name. He treats their fusion of strict religion with practical self-government as the seed from which much of American civilization grew.

snapshots.name: Indigenous Peoples ("the Indians")
snapshots.subtitle: Described as vanishing before European advance
snapshots.body: The peoples Tocqueville describes as native to the continent before European settlement, distinct in physical type and language from Europeans, Asiatics, and Africans alike. He treats their displacement and decline as one of the somber undercurrents of American expansion.

snapshots.name: Enslaved and Free Black Americans ("the Negroes")
snapshots.subtitle: Democracy's most dangerous contradiction
snapshots.body: The population Tocqueville treats as democracy's gravest internal threat: subject to slavery in the South and to entrenched prejudice even where free in the North, their fate he calls inseparably interwoven with that of the white population around them.

snapshots.name: The Tyranny of the Majority
snapshots.subtitle: Tocqueville's central warning
snapshots.body: The danger Tocqueville identifies as democracy's specific vulnerability: a majority whose power is so complete that no institution or law can check it once it forms a settled opinion, leaving individuals and minorities with no recourse against its pressure.

snapshots.name: Individualism
snapshots.subtitle: A word Tocqueville says he had to coin
snapshots.body: A term Tocqueville introduces because he says no exact equivalent existed before democracy produced the thing itself: a calm, deliberate withdrawal from public concerns into the small circle of family and friends, distinct from mere selfishness and, he argues, peculiar to democratic ages.
